title: Working at Height — Ladders, EWPs and Roofs
verdict:
I would not sign this and send a crew out on it today. It is a strong document — much stronger than most — and the legislation in it is, with two exceptions, genuinely correct. I checked every Queensland citation against the consolidated text on legislation.qld.gov.au and every one of the s 291 quotes is verbatim. What stops it is a hole in the emergency field and two steps that overstate how much protection they actually deliver.

WHAT I VERIFIED AND FOUND SOUND (so the author does not re-litigate it)
- hrcw: all six s 291 quotes are verbatim against the current reprint — (a), (d), (f), (k), (n), (o). Correct.
- s 289(2)(e) and the s 289(3)(d) "minor nature" exclusion: quoted accurately.
- ss 78, 79(3) (with the combination note), 80(2)-(4), 54, 55(3)(a), 213, 299(4), 300(2), 302, 303, 316, 317(1)-(2), 425(5)-(6), 427, 445, sch 3 item 21, sch 19 "scaffolding work" (>4m): all confirmed, all saying what the document says they say.
- The whole 306 series: 306C(2)(a), 306D(2)(a), 306D(3), 306E(4)(a)(i)-(ii) and (5)(a)-(c), 306F, 306G(1)-(5), 306I(1)-(4), (7)-(8), (11), (13), 306K(2)(a), 306L(3)(a)-(b) and (4), 306M(1)(a)-(e), (6), (7), (8). Every one checks out, including the detail that s 306M(1)(e)(ii) gives the 9.2m limit to an extension ladder used for electrical work.
- WHS Act ss 35, 36(a), 37(f) and (g), 38, 39, 47-49: all confirmed. 1300 362 128 is the WHSQ number.
- Electrical Safety Act 2002 s 18 (meaning of electrical work) and s 55 (licence to perform or supervise): confirmed.
- Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld): the repeal has been handled properly — no 2013 citations survive anywhere. I confirmed s 10 and schedule 2 (the header of schedule 2 reads "section 10(2)"), and the operating-plant figures quoted are right off the untrained-person table: 3,000mm for low voltage through to 132kV, 6,000mm above 132kV to 330kV, 8,000mm above 330kV. Part 3 division 3 is "Roof space work" and does apply only to BCA class 1, 2 and 10a — the summary of s 33(1)-(3) in step 3 is accurate. Part 8 division 3 s 196(1) and (2)(a) say exactly what the document paraphrases: tested by a competent person to decide whether it is energised, every exposed part treated as energised until isolated and found not to be.
- ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.5 is real, it is "First Aid Management of Harness Suspension Trauma", and it says what the document says: trauma "reported to affect people who are suspended within a body harness for a prolonged period of time (more than 10 min)", position of comfort "ideally lying down", and of the old rule — "Some agencies have previously recommended that those with suspension trauma are maintained in a sitting position and avoid lying flat for 30 minutes. This review has found no evidence to support this practice and it may be harmful." Quoted faithfully.
- JSON shape: exact match to SwmsTemplate, no extra keys, no suggestFor, id is "heights". Every step passes the ordering rule (highest-first), no residual exceeds its initial, and no step is administrative/PPE-only claiming low.

WHAT STOPS IT
The fatal one is electricity. The word "shock" does not appear anywhere in this document. The SWMS puts a technician's head into an energised ceiling void, runs a boom near overhead lines, names s 291(k) as a reason this is high risk construction work, and then gives the crew no emergency response for the one event those controls exist to prevent. The instinctive reaction — grab him, touch the machine, run in — is what kills the second person, and this statement does not say so. It also does not know that an electrical incident is notified to a different regulator: ESR 2026 s 292(1) requires a PCBU to notify the electrical safety regulator immediately of a serious electrical incident or dangerous electrical event, and ES Act s 11 makes a shock treated by or under a doctor's supervision exactly that. The NOTIFICATION paragraph names only WHSQ.

The second omission is heat. The document twice tells the crew a Queensland roof space will be over 50°C and warns about metal deck in summer, then offers no first aid or escalation when someone goes down from it.

Then two credibility problems. Step 5 (work from the EWP) rates the crush hazard extreme — correctly calling it the way most EWP fatalities happen — and lands on medium off one engineering control it simply assumes is fitted, plus seven administrative rules. Step 7 handles the same problem honestly (extreme to high plus a hold point). Step 5 should do the same. And step 6 labels a harness-and-locking-device on a ladder rail as "engineering" and ranks it above the administrative controls, which contradicts the document's own correct instruction, made twice elsewhere, that harness systems are PPE at the bottom of s 79(3).

One citation is wrong in a way a technician will act on. Step 0 tells the crew to demand a six-monthly written inspection record for the roof anchor and cites s 306I(10)(c). That paragraph reads "a competent person inspects the components of the system, other than each anchorage point" — anchorage points are expressly carved out of it. The building manager will correctly say no such record is required, and the technician has no answer. The right authority is s 306I(1): each anchorage point must be engineer-designed for the purpose, or inspected and approved by a competent person before first use. Keep the company rule, fix the section.

One thing I could not check, and am not going to pretend otherwise: I could not reach the Standards Australia store or worksafe.qld.gov.au from here (404 and a Cloudflare challenge). So the standards editions — AS 2550.10:2025, AS/NZS 1418.10:2025, AS/NZS 1891.4:2025, AS 5532:2025, AS 1670.1:2024, AS/NZS 2865:2009 Amd 1:2025 — and the exact Queensland code of practice titles remain unverified by me. I am not calling any of them wrong. Somebody with access needs to confirm them against the Standards Australia catalogue before this is signed, because I cannot.

Fix the emergency field, re-rate step 5, re-level step 6's ladder control, correct the anchor citation, put solar on the roof, and this is a document I would sign.

blocking.problem: No response at all for electric shock or electrocution. The word "shock" appears zero times in the entire document, yet the SWMS names contact with lighting circuits at ceiling level, unidentified live wiring and open junction boxes in ceiling voids, work on or beside mains circuits, the FIP and switchboards, and overhead electric lines within reach of a boom — and lists s 291(k) ("is carried out on or near energised electrical installations or services") as one of its six HRCW triggers. There is no instruction on what to do when a technician is shocked in a ceiling void, and none for the scenario the schedule 2 exclusion-zone control exists to prevent: an EWP contacting an overhead line. That is the case where the instinctive act — climbing out, touching the machine, running in to help — kills the rescuer. Separately, the NOTIFICATION paragraph names only Workplace Health and Safety Queensland. Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 292(1) reads: "A person who conducts a business or undertaking must ensure the regulator is notified immediately after becoming aware that a serious electrical incident or dangerous electrical event arising out of the conduct of the business or undertaking has occurred" (maximum penalty 100 penalty units), and Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) s 11 makes a person who "receives a shock or injury from electricity, and is treated for the shock or injury by or under the supervision of a doctor" a serious electrical incident. That is a separate regulator and a separate immediate duty this statement does not mention.
blocking.fix: Add an ELECTRIC SHOCK / CONTACT WITH AN ELECTRIC LINE paragraph to emergency. It must say: do not touch the person or the plant; isolate the supply if you can reach a point of isolation safely, otherwise treat everything as live. If the EWP or its boom is in contact with an overhead line, the operator STAYS IN THE BASKET and does not touch the basket and any other surface at the same time; nobody on the ground approaches the machine, the ground or anything touching it; keep everyone back at least the schedule 2 exclusion-zone distance and ring the supply authority and 000 immediately, and do not attempt recovery or lowering until the line is confirmed isolated. Only if fire in the basket forces it does the operator jump clear without touching the machine and the ground together, landing with feet together, then shuffle away with feet in contact. Once the person is clear and the supply is proved off: start CPR, get the defib on. Then add to the NOTIFICATION paragraph that any electric shock treated by or under a doctor's supervision, and any dangerous electrical event, is notified immediately to the electrical safety regulator under the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) — a separate call from the WHSQ notification, not a substitute for it.

blocking.problem: No heat illness or heat stroke response, in a document that twice identifies severe heat as a hazard and describes the exposure precisely. Step 3 hazards include "Severe heat load in a Queensland roof space in the afternoon" and its control states a roof space "will be well over 50°C"; step 7 hazards include "Heat stress on a metal deck in a Queensland summer" and its control says "a technician who has stopped sweating comes down now" — which is a description of heat stroke, a medical emergency with a high fatality rate if it is not cooled fast. The document tells the crew to recognise it and then gives them nothing to do about it. There is no cooling instruction, no threshold for calling 000, and no plan for retrieving a collapsed technician from a ceiling void or a roof, which is itself a rescue problem given the crew is two people and one of them is down.
blocking.fix: Add a HEAT ILLNESS paragraph to emergency: get them out of the void or off the roof and into shade or air conditioning immediately, using the EWP or the access route already planned; lay them down and elevate the legs; strip outer clothing and PPE; cool aggressively with water, wet cloths and airflow, and do not wait to see if they improve. Call 000 for any confused, staggering, vomiting or unconscious technician, or anyone who has stopped sweating on a hot roof — those are heat stroke, and cooling starts before the ambulance arrives, not after. Note that a technician down in a ceiling void or on a roof is a retrieval as well as a medical problem, and that the second person calls for help before attempting a retrieval alone.

blocking.field: steps[6].hazards and steps[7].hazards (and the controls under both)
blocking.problem: Rooftop solar PV is not controlled anywhere. The string "solar" appears exactly once in the whole document — in steps[1].hazards, as "Overhead electric lines, solar arrays and unfused mains across the yard or carpark" — which frames it as a ground-level obstacle for driving an EWP. Neither of the two roof steps ("Get onto the roof", "Work on the roof — edges, skylights and fragile sheeting") mentions it in a hazard or a control. On a 2026 Queensland commercial roof, an array is the normal case, and the roof-mounted booster, tank top, plant deck or detector the technician has come for is routinely on the far side of it. The specific danger is that PV DC strings are energised by daylight and are NOT killed by the building's main switch or by anything the site can isolate for you — so every other electrical control in this statement ("isolated by a licensed electrical worker, locked out, PROVED de-energised") does not apply to them. On top of that the array creates trip hazards from rails, conduit and cable trays, hides fragile sheeting and roof penetrations under panels, blocks the walkway the document tells the crew to stay on, and puts degraded DC cabling at hand height.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[6].hazards and steps[7].hazards a line naming rooftop solar PV: live DC that cannot be isolated by the site, damaged or degraded DC cabling and combiner boxes, and rails, conduit and panels obstructing the walkway and hiding fragile sheeting. Add an administrative control to step 7: ask at the pre-day call whether the roof has an array and where it sits relative to the work; do not touch, lean on, step on, walk between or move any panel, rail, conduit, combiner box or DC cable; treat all PV cabling as live regardless of what any switch is set to, because the array is energised by daylight; if the only route to the device runs through the array or the array's cabling is damaged, stop and ring the supervisor for a licensed electrical worker and a route, and add a matching siteSpecificPrompt.

blocking.field: steps[5].residualRisk ("Work from the EWP at the detector, head or valve")
blocking.problem: initialRisk is extreme and residualRisk is medium — a two-level drop — on a step whose lead hazard is "Crushing between the basket rail and overhead pipework, racking, ducting or a beam — the way most EWP fatalities happen". Of the eight controls, the isolate control is a drop-zone barrier that protects people underneath, not the operator, and six of the remaining seven are administrative work rules (look up, move on one axis, approach from beside, spotter, no travel elevated, nothing handed over the rail). The only control that actually acts on the crush mechanism is the engineering one, and it is written as an assumption: "Secondary guarding — anti-entrapment bar or pressure-sensing plate — stays fitted and working. Never fold it out of the way to get closer to a head." It never asks whether the machine has any. Most scissor lifts and a large share of hire booms do not, and the step gives the technician no instruction for that case. Compare steps[7], which handles the identical problem honestly: extreme down to high, with a named HOLD POINT requiring the supervisor's sign-off and an additional control on the day. Step 5 claims a bigger reduction on weaker controls with no hold point.
blocking.fix: Either set residualRisk to "high" for this step and add a HOLD POINT control in the same form as steps[7] (supervisor sign-off on the day naming an additional control, or the job is rebooked with different access), or add an engineering control before the administrative ones requiring that a boom used to work under or beside overhead structure has working secondary guarding, checked at pre-start, and that a machine without it is not positioned under pipework, racking, ducting or a beam. If both go in, medium becomes arguable; with neither, it is not.

blocking.problem: A fall arrest harness system is labelled "engineering" and, because of that label, is ranked above every administrative control in the step. The control reads: "On a steep fixed ladder, clip to the ladder-mounted anchorage line or rail at the BASE before you leave the ground, locking device on the front attachment point, and the shortest lanyard the system takes so a slip is caught immediately rather than after a metre." A harness with a locking device on a line or rail is the fall arrest harness system defined in s 306A, and s 79(3) puts a fall arrest system last — after a fall prevention device and after a work positioning system. The document knows this and says so twice elsewhere in its own words: steps[4].controls[8] says of the basket harness "it is PPE — the bottom of the s 79(3) ranking, not an isolation control", and steps[7] correctly levels both travel restraint and fall arrest as "ppe". This one control contradicts the rest of the statement and mis-teaches the hierarchy at the exact point a technician is deciding what to rely on.
blocking.fix: Change steps[6].controls[1].level from "engineering" to "ppe" and move it to the end of the controls array so the ordering rule still passes. Keep the wording — clipping on at the base before leaving the ground is right and matches s 306I(3), which requires the anchorage point to be positioned so the lanyard can be attached before the person moves into a position where they could fall. If the building has a compliant fixed stair or a caged ladder to AS 1657, that is the fall prevention device and belongs above it, not below.

blocking.field: steps[0].controls[3].control ("Plan the access before the day, from the office")
blocking.problem: Wrong section cited for the roof anchor inspection record, and the section says the opposite of what is claimed. The control reads: "The Regulation requires a competent person to inspect harness-based systems at least every 6 months and to give a written record — s 306G(4) for travel restraint, s 306I(10)(c) for a fall arrest harness system. If nobody can produce a record, the anchor is not used." The s 306G(4) half is right. But s 306I(10)(c) reads: "at least once every 6 months, a competent person inspects the components of the system, other than each anchorage point, and gives the person a written record of the inspection". Anchorage points are expressly carved out of that duty, and the control is being used to demand a record for the anchor. In the field the building manager will correctly answer that no such record is required for the anchor, and the technician has cited a section that proves the manager's point rather than his own. The obligation that does attach to an anchor is s 306I(1): each anchorage point must be "designed by an engineer for the purpose for which it is intended to be used" or "inspected and approved by a competent person before the anchorage point is first used by any person", and s 306I(10)(b) requires an anchorage point not be used if a competent person considers it worn or its load-bearing capacity may be impaired.
blocking.fix: Rewrite the citation: for a fall arrest anchor, cite s 306I(1) — engineer-designed for the purpose, or inspected and approved by a competent person before first use — and s 306I(10)(b). Keep s 306G(4) for travel restraint systems, and keep s 306I(10)(c) only where the control is about harnesses, lanyards and connectors (as steps[7] already does correctly). The company rule "if nobody can produce a record, the anchor is not used" is good practice and should stay, but say plainly that it is a company rule sitting on top of the s 306I(1) duty, not a quotation from s 306I(10)(c).

blocking.field: steps[1].controls[1].level ("Sign in and walk the area before anything goes up")
blocking.problem: Keeping clear of an overhead electric line is levelled "engineering". Maintaining a separation distance is a work rule that depends entirely on the operator's judgment of a distance to a conductor that will kill on contact — that is administrative. The genuinely higher-order control is in the last sentence of the same item ("the line is isolated or covered by the supply authority BEFORE the machine moves"), which is isolation, and it is buried at the end of a long paragraph where it reads as the fallback rather than the answer. The schedule 2 figures quoted are correct — I checked them against the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) untrained-person table for operating plant and they match — so this is a levelling and emphasis problem, not a wrong number.
blocking.fix: Split the item. Make the supply authority isolation or line covering its own "isolate" control, placed first. Leave the exclusion-zone distances as an "administrative" control below it. While splitting, tighten the on-foot figures: the document says "3m off any line you have not had consultation about, and 3m up to 132kV", which is right as far as it goes, but the untrained-person on-foot zone rises to 4,500mm above 132kV to 220kV, 5,000mm above 220kV to 275kV and 6,000mm above 275kV — worth stating rather than leaving to the "assume the largest zone" catch-all.

blocking.field: steps[3].controls[5].level ("Platform ladder and mobile scaffold work in corridors, plant rooms and ceiling spaces")
blocking.problem: A prohibition is levelled "engineering". The control is "Never use a ladder to support a platform or a plank... s 306M(7): the person must not use, or allow another person to use, the ladder to support a platform." The quotation of s 306M(7) is accurate. But a rule that says never do this is administrative — nothing physical stops it happening. It is ranked above the eight administrative controls purely on the strength of the label.
blocking.fix: Change level to "administrative" and move it into the administrative block. The substance is correct and important — leave the wording and the s 306M(7) quote alone.

blocking.problem: Two small citation slips. First, references says s 306A includes definitions of "free fall and limited free fall". It does not — s 306A defines anchorage point, edge protection, fall arrest harness system, fall arresting platform, fall protection cover, housing construction work, permitted work, static line and travel restraint system. "free fall" and "limited free fall" are defined in s 306I(14). Second, whenRequired says of s 306I(13) "It is penalty-backed." No maximum penalty is attached to s 306I(13) itself; within s 306I only subsections (7) and (9) carry one. Non-compliance is picked up indirectly through s 306C(4)/306D(4) ("the control measure and the use of the control measure must comply with this subdivision. Maximum penalty—60 penalty units"). Related: steps[0].controls[2] and steps[7].controls[6] state the solo rule as "no harness is worn alone — s 306I(13)", but s 306I(13) governs only a fall arrest harness system as defined in s 306A. It does not reach a travel restraint system, which is governed by s 306G and carries no solo prohibition — and travel restraint is precisely what this statement recommends most often on a roof. The company rule ("no solo roof access at all, whatever system is worn") is stated separately and clearly, so nobody is going to be misled into working alone; but the legal claim is broader than the section.
blocking.fix: Move "free fall" and "limited free fall" to a s 306I(14) reference. Replace "It is penalty-backed" with a plain statement that compliance with the subdivision is enforced through ss 306C(4) and 306D(4). Where the solo rule is stated, say that s 306I(13) prohibits solo use of a fall arrest harness system, and that the no-solo-roof rule for travel restraint is Safe QLD company policy on top of it — which is what whenRequired already says correctly and the two step controls state too loosely.

blocking.problem: I could not verify a single standards edition from this session and I am not going to assert one way or the other. The Standards Australia store returned nothing fetchable and worksafe.qld.gov.au is behind a Cloudflare challenge. So these remain unchecked: AS 2550.10:2025 (and its claim to supersede AS 2550.10-2006), AS/NZS 1418.10:2025, AS/NZS 1891.4:2025 (and its claim to supersede AS/NZS 1891.4:2009), AS 5532:2025 (and its claim to supersede AS/NZS 5532:2013), AS 1670.1:2024 (and its claim to supersede AS 1670.1:2018), AS 1851-2012 (Amd 1:2016) being the current edition, AS/NZS 2865:2009 (Amd 1:2025), AS 1891.3:2020 (Amd 1:2021), AS 1891.5:2020, AS 1892.1:2018, AS 1892.5:2020 (Amd 1:2021), AS 2118.1:2017 (Amd 2:2020), AS 2419.1:2021, AS 1657:2018, AS/NZS 1891.1:2020, and the exact titles and years of the three Queensland codes of practice. Two also carry an AS versus AS/NZS prefix risk that is easy to get wrong: AS 1891.3 / AS 1891.5 and AS/NZS 2865 versus AS 2865. Note this is a caveat, not a finding — I have no evidence any of them is wrong.
blocking.fix: Before this is signed, have someone with Standards Australia catalogue access confirm each designation, edition year and supersession claim, and confirm the three code of practice titles and years against worksafe.qld.gov.au. Anything that cannot be confirmed should be named without a year ("the current edition of AS 2550.10") rather than carrying a year that might be invented. Note that steps[3].controls[10] and steps[6].controls[5] each cite a ladder standard obligation only through the Regulation, which is the right instinct and needs no change.

blocking.field: permits and siteSpecificPrompts (roof space work in class 1, 2 and 10a buildings)
blocking.problem: steps[3].controls[12] correctly summarises Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) part 3 division 3 — that in a class 1, 2 or 10a building the relevant electrical installation must be de-energised before a worker enters the roof space unless one of the s 33(2) circumstances applies, and that a recorded risk assessment and a written statement of hazards and controls must then be prepared first. But nothing in permits or siteSpecificPrompts triggers the crew to actually produce those two documents, and this bites constantly in fire protection: a class 2 building is an ordinary apartment block with detection and sprinklers. The duty carries 60 penalty units on the business under s 33 and 10 penalty units on the worker personally under s 34, and s 36 requires the risk assessment be kept at least 28 days after the work and the statement until the work is complete. A technician who reads step 3 will know the rule exists and still have no prompt on the day to check whether the building is class 2 or whether the paperwork was done.
blocking.fix: Add a permits entry along the lines of: "Roof space entry in a class 1, 2 or 10a building — recorded risk assessment and written statement of hazards and controls under the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) roof space provisions, prepared before entry and kept per that regulation." Add a matching siteSpecificPrompt: "Is this building class 1, 2 or 10a, and are you entering a roof space? If yes, is the installation de-energised — and if it cannot be, who did the recorded risk assessment and where is the written statement?"
